A 63-year-old male patient is admitted for a repeat right knee replacement. His medical history includes
lumbar radiculopathy and rotator cuff tendonitis, for which he takes acetaminophen, gabapentin,
methadone, and extended-release oxycodone. He receives a femoral nerve block with a continuous
infusion catheter and continues his usual medications. The surgery is performed under general
anesthesia without complications. In the post-anesthesia care unit, the patient reports severe,
uncontrolled pain despite receiving standard doses of fentanyl, hydromorphone, and oxycodone, as
well as activation of his nerve catheter. His vital signs include a temperature of 98.6°F (37°C), blood
pressure of 196/111 mmHg, pulse of 87/min, and respiratory rate of 26/min. The right knee is braced,
with no significant localized edema or erythema observed. What is the most appropriate next step?
Answer Choices: (A) Refer to a pain specialist for refractory postoperative pain (B) Administer more
fentanyl (C) Administer ketamine for opioid-refractory pain (D) Wait for preoperative methadone to take
effect (E) Discontinue all opioids and trial non-pharmacologic therapy (F) Administer intravenous
acetaminophen for multimodal analgesia (G) Apply topical lidocaine patch to knee (H) Transition to oral
morphine for better pain control (I) Perform imaging to rule out compartment syndrome (J) Increase the
rate of the femoral nerve catheter infusion
 A. Discontinue all opioids and trial non-pharmacologic therapy
B. Transition to oral morphine for better pain control
C. Refer to a pain specialist for refractory postoperative pain
D. Administer more fentanyl
E. Increase the rate of the femoral nerve catheter infusion
F. Apply topical lidocaine patch to knee
G. Wait for preoperative methadone to take effect
H. Perform imaging to rule out compartment syndrome
I. Administer ketamine for opioid-refractory pain
J. Administer intravenous acetaminophen for multimodal analgesia
